ankle_pumps: Lie or sit with the leg straight.
Pull toes up towards you, then point them away.
Moves swelling out after injury or surgery.
quad_set: Sit or lie with the leg straight and a rolled towel under the knee.
Tighten the thigh to press the back of the knee into the towel.
Watch the kneecap glide up as the muscle switches on.
slr: Lie on your back, other knee bent.
Lock the straight knee with a quad set first.
Lift the leg to the height of the other knee, lower slowly.
If the knee bends during the lift (a 'lag'), go back to quad sets.
heel_slide: Slide the heel towards your bottom as far as comfortable.
Use a towel around the foot to help if needed.
prone_hang: Lie face down with the kneecap just off the end of the bed.
Full straightening early is one of the most important goals after ACL surgery.
patellar_mob: Sit with the leg straight and thigh relaxed.
Gently glide the kneecap up, down, in and out with your fingers.
Hold each direction a few seconds.
Only after surgery when your surgeon or physio has cleared it.
mini_squat: Feet hip-width, hold a support if needed.
Sit back a little as if to a high chair, knees to about 45°.
Push through both heels to stand.
Knees track over the 2nd toe, not caving in.
wall_sit: Back against a wall, slide down to a pain-free knee angle.
Isometric holds often reduce knee and tendon pain for a while afterwards.
spanish_squat: Loop a strong band behind both knees and anchor it to a post.
Lean back into the band and sit down until shins are vertical.
A go-to exercise for jumper's knee (patellar tendinopathy).
tke: Vastus medialis, last degrees of extension
Band around the back of the knee, anchored in front.
Start with the knee slightly bent.
Push the knee back to fully straight against the band, squeeze 2 s.
Slow and controlled, no snapping into lock.
step_up: Step up with the working leg and stand tall.
Step down slowly with the other leg.
Raise the step height as strength improves.
step_down: Stand on a step on the working leg.
Slowly lower the other heel to touch the floor in front.
Push back up without locking the knee hard.
Knee stays in line with the foot. Use a mirror.
split_squat: Long stride stance, back heel up.
Lower the back knee straight down towards the floor.
Drive up through the front heel.
Front knee may go over the toes; keep it in line with the foot.
bulgarian: Back foot on a bench behind you.
Lower down on the front leg under control.
Drive up through the front foot.
Add dumbbells or a backpack when 3×10 is easy.
squat: Feet shoulder-width (hold a weight at the chest to progress).
Sit down between the heels to a pain-free depth.
3 s down, 3 s up builds strength in tendons too.
decline_squat: Stand on one leg on a 25° slope (decline board or wedge).
Use the other leg to help come back up if needed.
bridge: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat.
Squeeze glutes and lift hips into a straight line.
Push through heels; don't arch the low back.
sl_bridge: Bridge position, lift one foot off the floor.
Hips stay level like a table.
clamshell: Lie on your side, knees bent, heels together.
Open the top knee without rolling the pelvis back.
Add a band above the knees for progression.
hip_abd: Lie on your side, bottom knee bent.
Lift the straight top leg slightly behind the body.
Strong hip abductors reduce knee 'caving in'.
sl_rdl: Stand on one leg with a soft knee.
Hinge forward, the free leg going back, back flat.
Return to standing by squeezing the glute.
Hold a wall at first. Hips stay square to the floor.
hip_hinge: Hold a stick along your spine touching head, upper back and tailbone.
Push the hips back, keeping all 3 contact points.
The safe way to bend and lift.
slider_curl: Lie on your back, heels on towels on a smooth floor.
Slide the heels out slowly, then pull them back in.
Start with two legs, progress to one.
nordic: Kneel with a partner holding your ankles.
Lower your body forward as slowly as possible, hips straight.
Catch yourself with your hands, push back up.
One of the best-proven hamstring injury preventers in football.
iso_ham: Lie on your back, knee bent at about 30°.
Dig the heel into the floor at low effort (30–50%).
Should feel like work, not pain.
strides: Reach the target speed in the middle third.
jog: Each pain-free session, add jog time.
Run on flat, even ground first.
bike: Seat high enough that the knee is almost straight at the bottom.
Rock back and forth first if a full turn is not yet possible.
walk: Walk on flat ground at a pace that raises breathing.
Keep posture tall and arms swinging.
For low back pain, walking is one of the best treatments.
pogo: Small quick hops on both feet, knees nearly straight.
Stay on the balls of the feet.
drop_land: Step off a low box (20–30 cm).
Land on both feet softly, hips back, knees over toes.
Quiet landings mean good shock absorption.
lateral_bound: Jump sideways from one leg to the other.
Land and stick for 2 s before the next.
Knee must not cave inward on landing.
sl_hop: Land softly and hold for 3 s.
Progress distance, then add lateral and diagonal hops.
Compare distance with the uninjured leg — target 90%+.
agility: Finally unplanned cuts reacting to a partner's signal.
Unplanned cutting is the last step before full training.
copenhagen: Side plank with the top leg on a bench.
Short lever: knee on the bench. Long lever: ankle on the bench.
Lift hips and hold, bottom leg free.
Shown to cut groin injuries in football by around 40%.
adductor_squeeze: Lie on your back, knees bent, ball or fist between the knees.
Increase squeeze effort as pain allows.
side_lunge: Shift to one side, bending that knee, other leg straight.
Keep the bent knee in line with the foot.
hip_flexor_stretch: Half-kneel, back knee on a cushion.
Tuck the pelvis under and squeeze the back glute.
calf_raise: Stand on both feet, hold a support.
Rise high onto the balls of the feet.
Move to the edge of a step for more range.
sl_calf_raise: Stand on one foot, light hand support.
bent_knee_calf: Stand with knees bent about 30° (or seated with weight on the knees).
Rise onto the toes keeping the knee bend.
The soleus takes huge load when running.
iso_calf: Rise onto the toes halfway on one or two legs.
Helps settle Achilles pain before heavier loading.
eccentric_heel_drop: Stand on a step on the balls of both feet.
Shift onto the injured leg and lower the heel slowly over 3 s.
Use both legs to come back up.
Insertional (heel-bone) pain: don't drop below step level.
band_4way: Sit with a band around the forefoot.
Push down, pull up, turn in, turn out against the band.
Eversion (turning out) is the key one after a sprain.
ankle_abc: Sit with the foot off the floor.
Draw the alphabet with your big toe.
Move from the ankle, not the knee.
knee_to_wall: Face a wall, toes a few cm away.
Drive the knee to touch the wall, heel down.
Move the foot back as range improves.
Normal is about 10 cm toe-to-wall. Compare both sides.
calf_stretch: Hands on a wall, injured leg behind.
Then bend the back knee to stretch the soleus.
sl_balance: Stand on one leg, knee soft.
Progress: eyes closed → on a pillow → catching a ball.
Balance training reduces repeat ankle sprains.
star_reach: Reach the other foot forward, back-left, back-right as far as you can.
short_foot: Sit or stand with the foot flat.
Pull the ball of the foot towards the heel to raise the arch, toes relaxed.
towel_scrunch: Curl the toes to pull the towel towards you.
Spread the toes wide at the end.
Add a light weight on the towel later.
plantar_stretch: Sit and cross the leg over the other knee.
Pull the toes back towards the shin.
Feel a stretch in the arch.
Do this before your first steps in the morning.
ball_roll: Roll the arch over a ball or frozen water bottle.
A frozen bottle also helps calm pain.
rathleff: Single-leg heel raise: 3 s up, 2 s hold, 3 s down.
Add a backpack with books as it gets easy.
tib_raise: Lean back against a wall, heels 30 cm away.
Lift the toes and forefoot towards the shins.
Strengthens the shin muscles that suffer in shin splints.
cat_camel: Slowly round the back up, then let it sag gently.
Mobility, not stretching. Keep it gentle.
dead_bug: On your back, arms up, hips and knees at 90°.
Lower opposite arm and leg slowly.
Keep the low back gently against the floor.
Breathe out as the limbs lower.
bird_dog: Reach opposite arm and leg out long.
Hold 5–10 s, don't rotate the hips.
Imagine a cup of tea on your lower back.
mcgill_curl: On your back, one knee bent, hands under the low back.
Lift head and shoulders just off the floor, neck still.
The low back stays in its natural curve.
side_plank: On your side, elbow under the shoulder.
Knees bent first, then straight legs.
Lift hips into a line and hold.
Head, hips, feet in one line.
open_book: Lie on your side, knees bent, arms together in front.
Open the top arm across to the other side, following it with your eyes.
kb_deadlift: Hinge at the hips, flat back, grab the handle.
Gradual loading builds a stronger, less sensitive back.
carry: Hold a heavy weight in one hand.
Walk tall for 20–30 m without leaning.
pendulum: Lean forward with a hand on a table.
Let the sore arm hang loose.
Make small circles by swaying your body.
Arm stays relaxed — the body moves it.
scap_squeeze: Draw shoulder blades back and down.
No shrugging up to the ears.
wall_slide: Forearms on a wall, elbows at shoulder height.
Slide arms up the wall in a pain-free range.
Stop below the point of pain.
er_band: Elbow at your side, towel under it, band in hand.
ir_band: Elbow at your side, band anchored to the outside.
Rotate the forearm in towards the belly.
pull_apart: Hold a band at shoulder height, arms straight.
Pull the band apart to touch the chest.
Ribs down, don't arch the back.
wall_pushup: Hands on a wall at shoulder height, body straight.
Bend the elbows to bring the chest to the wall.
Push back, then push a little further to spread the shoulder blades.
The 'plus' at the end protects the shoulder.
db_press: Sit or stand with light dumbbells at shoulder height.
Press up in a pain-free arc.
Start light; pain should stay 3/10 or lower.
wrist_iso: Forearm on a table, palm down, hand off the edge.
Push the back of the hand up against your other hand.
ecc_wrist: Forearm on a table, palm down, light dumbbell.
Use the other hand to lift the wrist up.
Mild discomfort is OK; sharp pain is not.
pron_sup: Hold a hammer by the handle, elbow at 90°.
Slowly rotate palm up then palm down.
Hold lower on the handle to make it easier.
grip: Squeeze a soft ball or towel.
Squeeze with the elbow straight later in rehab.
forearm_stretch: Arm straight in front, palm down.
Gently bend the wrist down with the other hand.
pushup: Hands under shoulders, body in a straight line (knees down to make it easier).
Lower the chest towards the floor.
Push back up without the hips sagging.
Too hard? Start with wall push-ups.
plank: Forearms on the floor, elbows under shoulders.
Lift into a straight line from head to heels.
Squeeze glutes; don't let the hips sag.
superman: Lift arms, chest and legs slightly off the floor.
Small lift is enough — no cranking the neck.
jumping_jack: Jump the feet wide while raising the arms overhead.
Low-impact version: step one foot out at a time.
march: Lift one knee to hip height, then the other.
reverse_lunge: Step one foot back and lower the back knee towards the floor.
Push through the front heel to return.
Easier on the knees than forward lunges.
sit_to_stand: Sit on the front of a chair, feet flat.
Lean forward and stand up without using your hands.
The most useful leg exercise for daily life.
mountain_climber: High plank position, hands under shoulders.
Drive one knee towards the chest, then switch.
Slow it down to make it a core exercise.
neck_mob: Slowly nod down and up, then turn left and right.
Great break from phone and desk work.
chest_stretch: Forearm on a door frame, elbow at shoulder height.
Step through gently until you feel the chest stretch.
ham_stretch: Lie on your back with a towel around one foot.
Lift the straight leg until you feel a stretch.
Keep the other leg flat or bent — whatever is comfortable.
arm_circles: Make slow circles forward, then backward.
Keep the shoulders down away from the ears.
sl_squat: Stand on one leg in front of a box or chair.
Slowly sit back until you lightly touch the box.
Stand up on the same leg, knee in line with the 2nd toe.
Use a higher box to make it easier.
monster_walk: Band around the knees or ankles, knees slightly bent.
Step sideways, keeping tension on the band.
Toes point forward; don't let the knees cave in.
leg_ext: Straighten one knee fully and squeeze the thigh for 2 s.
Add an ankle weight to progress. After ACL surgery, ask your surgeon when this is allowed.
heel_walk: Lift the toes and walk on your heels.
Keep the knees straight and stand tall.
toe_walk: Rise high onto the balls of your feet.
Walk forward without letting the heels drop.
Keep the ankles straight, not rolling out.
quad_stretch: Bend the top knee and hold the ankle.
Pull the heel towards your bottom, keeping the knees together.
Push the hip slightly forward to feel more stretch.
chin_tuck: Sit or stand tall, eyes level.
Glide the chin straight back (make a 'double chin').
Don't nod down — slide straight back.
neck_iso: Place your hand against the side of your head.
Gently push the head into the hand without moving.
Hold 5–10 s. Repeat front, back and both sides.
band_row: Hinge forward with a flat back, weights or band in hands.
Pull the elbows back, squeezing the shoulder blades.
Keep the neck long and the back flat.
prone_y: Lie face down on a bench or the floor.
Lift the arms out to a 'T', then up to a 'Y', thumbs up.
side_er: Lie on your side, towel under the top elbow, elbow bent 90°.
Rotate the forearm up towards the ceiling.
One of the best-studied rotator cuff exercises.
press_up: Lie face down, hands under the shoulders.
Push the chest up, keeping the hips on the floor.
Helpful when bending forward hurts; stop if leg pain increases.
knee_to_chest: Pull one knee to your chest with both hands.
Breathe out and relax the back.
child_pose: Kneel and sit back towards your heels.
Reach the arms forward on the floor.
Relax and breathe into the back.
A cushion between heels and bottom helps if knees are stiff.
pallof_press: Stand side-on to a band anchored at chest height.
Hold the band at your chest, then press it straight out.
Hold 2 s without twisting, bring it back.
The trunk must not rotate towards the anchor.
bridge_march: Lift one foot a little off the floor, then the other.
Keep the hips level the whole time.
If the hips drop, go back to normal bridges.
side_add: Lie on your side, top leg bent in front.
Lift the straight bottom leg up off the floor.
toe_yoga: Lift only the big toe, keeping the others down.
Then lift the other four, keeping the big toe down.
Hard at first — it improves quickly.
glute_kickback: Kick one heel back and up to hip height.
Lower slowly without arching the back.
Squeeze the glute at the top.
hip_circles: Stand on one leg, hold a support.
Lift the other knee and draw big circles with it.
lateral_hop: Hop sideways over a line and land softly.
box_jump: Stand in front of a low box.
Swing the arms and jump onto the box, landing softly.
Land in a quiet half-squat, knees out.
skipping: Skip forward driving one knee up.
Land on the ball of the foot.
Swing the arms opposite to the legs.
Great warm-up before running and sprinting.
nerve_glide: Straighten the knee while lifting the head to look up.
Bend the knee while dropping the chin. Move slowly in rhythm.
Gentle movement only — a mild pull is fine, it should not increase leg pain afterwards.
thoracic_ext: Sit on a chair, hands behind your head.
Gently arch the upper back over the chair back, looking up.
Move from the upper back, not the low back.

INJ.name: ACL tear / reconstruction
INJ.what: The anterior cruciate ligament stops the shin sliding forward and twisting. It usually tears on a sudden stop, cut or awkward landing. Many athletes have reconstruction surgery; some recover without it.
signs: Pop at the moment of injury
Fast swelling within hours
Knee gives way when turning
flags: Knee locked and cannot straighten
Calf pain, heat and swelling after surgery (possible clot)
Fever or wound redness after surgery
INJ.note: Follow your surgeon's protocol first. Graft type and extra repairs (meniscus) change the timeline. Most guidelines advise at least 9 months before return to pivoting sport.

sev.d: Coper athletes or non-pivoting sport, guided by a physio.

phases.goal: Full knee straightening, wake up the quads, reduce swelling.
exit: Knee straightens fully (same as other side)
Straight leg raise with no knee bend

phases.goal: Normal gait, bend to 120°+, basic strength and balance.

exit: 10 controlled single-leg squats, knee in line
Quad strength at least 70% of the other leg
No swelling the day after training

phases.goal: Start running, jumping and landing safely.
exit: 20 min easy running without pain or swelling
Hop tests at least 90% of the other leg

phases.goal: Cutting, reaction and full team training.
exit: Confident in the knee — and cleared by surgeon/physio

INJ.name: Runner's knee (patellofemoral pain)
INJ.what: Pain around or behind the kneecap, worse on stairs, squatting, running downhill or sitting for long. Usually from load rising faster than the knee and hips can handle.
signs: Ache around the kneecap
Pain going downstairs
Pain after sitting with bent knees
flags: Big swelling
Knee locking or giving way
Pain at night or at rest that does not settle
INJ.note: Cut back (don't stop) running and jumping while pain settles. Hip and quad strength are the key to lasting relief.

sev.d: Ache after running or jumping, normal daily life.

phases.goal: Reduce pain with isometrics and hip work.
exit: Wall sit 45 s with little pain
No pain flare the next day
30 min running at 2/10 pain or less

INJ.name: Jumper's knee (patellar tendinopathy)
INJ.what: Overload of the tendon just below the kneecap. Pain is sharp and pin-point at the bottom of the kneecap during jumping, landing and deep squats.
signs: Pain at the bottom tip of the kneecap
Worse with jumping
Stiff in the morning, warms up then worsens
flags: Sudden pop and cannot straighten the knee (tendon rupture)
Big swelling
INJ.note: Tendons respond to progressive load, not rest. Total rest makes them weaker.

sev.d: Pain only after training, performance normal.
Stairs and squats hurt; sport stopped.

exit: Single-leg decline squat pain 3/10 or less

phases.goal: Build tendon capacity with slow heavy loading.
exit: Pain 3/10 or less during and next day
Full training with pain 2/10 or less

INJ.name: Meniscus tear
INJ.what: The menisci are two cartilage cushions in the knee. Tears come from twisting on a bent knee, or slowly with age. Many heal well with exercise alone.
signs: Pain on the inner or outer joint line
Swelling over a day
Catching, clicking, or difficulty squatting deep
flags: Knee locked and cannot straighten fully
Repeated giving way
INJ.note: After a meniscus REPAIR (stitches), surgeons usually limit deep bending and loaded squats for 6+ weeks. Follow their limits.

sev.d: Swelling after activity, deep squats hurt.

exit: Running, cutting and hopping without swelling

INJ.name: MCL sprain
INJ.what: The ligament on the inner side of the knee. Injured by a blow to the outside of the knee or the knee caving inward. Grades 1–2 heal well without surgery.
signs: Pain on the inner side of the knee
Pain when the knee is pushed inward
flags: Knee feels very loose
Big swelling within hours (may be ACL too)
INJ.note: Avoid side-to-side stress early. A hinged brace may be used for grade 2–3.

sev.d: Tender, but the knee feels stable.
Some looseness, painful to walk at first.

exit: Full range, no pain on inner knee during squats
Cutting and lateral bounds without pain

INJ.name: IT band syndrome
INJ.what: Pain on the outside of the knee, usually starting at the same distance into a run. Linked to training jumps and weak hip muscles.
signs: Sharp outer-knee pain while running
Worse running downhill
flags: Swelling inside the knee
Locking
INJ.note: Reduce running volume and downhill running while you strengthen the hips. Stretching the IT band alone rarely fixes it.

sev.d: Pain within 1–2 km or on stairs.

exit: Usual run distance without outer-knee pain

INJ.name: Ankle sprain
INJ.what: The most common sports injury. The foot rolls inward and stretches or tears the outer ankle ligaments. Proper rehab is key — without it, up to 1 in 3 people sprain it again.
signs: Swelling and bruising on the outer ankle
Pain putting weight on it
flags: Cannot take 4 steps at all
Tender on the bony knobs of the ankle or the outer foot bone (possible fracture — get an X-ray)
Numbness or a cold, pale foot
INJ.note: Use a brace or tape for sport for 6–12 months after return. Balance work is the single best protection against re-injury.

sev.d: Little swelling, can walk with mild pain.
Large swelling, unstable, very hard to walk.

phases.goal: Control swelling, keep moving, weight-bear as able.

INJ.name: Achilles tendinopathy
INJ.what: Overload of the Achilles tendon. Pain is 2–6 cm above the heel (mid-portion) or where the tendon meets the heel bone (insertional). Worst in the morning.
signs: Morning stiffness in the tendon
Thickening or tender lump
Pain at the start of running
flags: Sudden pop or feeling of being kicked in the heel (rupture)
Cannot rise onto the toes
INJ.note: Pain up to 3/10 during exercise is acceptable if it settles by the next morning.

sev.d: Stiff in the morning, fine once warm.
Pain in daily life, thickened tendon.

phases.goal: Settle pain while keeping the tendon loaded.
exit: Two-leg calf raise pain 3/10 or less
Full training, keep calf strength work

INJ.name: Plantar fasciitis (heel pain)
INJ.what: Pain under the heel from overload of the thick band (plantar fascia) along the arch. Classic sign: sharp pain on the first steps in the morning.
signs: Sharp heel pain on first steps
Eases after walking a few minutes
Worse after standing all day
flags: Numbness or tingling in the foot
Pain after a fall or jump (possible fracture)
Pain worse at night
INJ.note: Supportive shoes, no barefoot walking on hard floors early on. Strengthening speeds recovery.

INJ.name: Shin splints (MTSS)
INJ.what: Pain along the inner edge of the shin bone from bone and muscle overload, usually after a jump in running volume or hard surfaces.
signs: Diffuse pain along the inner shin (over 5 cm)
Hurts at the start of runs
flags: One small spot of severe bone pain (possible stress fracture)
Pain at rest or at night
Numbness or tight, swollen calf
INJ.note: Bone needs rest from impact but responds to strength work. Increase running by no more than 10% a week.

sev.d: Pain in daily life — rule out stress fracture first.

phases.goal: Rest from running, strengthen lower leg.

exit: Run 30 min pain-free on grass then road

INJ.name: Hamstring strain
INJ.what: A tear in the muscles at the back of the thigh, usually during sprinting or kicking. The most common injury in football, and it often comes back if rehab is rushed.
signs: Sudden sharp pain at the back of the thigh while sprinting
Pain bending the knee against resistance
Bruising
flags: Pop near the sitting bone with large bruising (possible tendon tear)
Cannot walk
INJ.note: Re-injury rates are high. Nordic curls and full-speed sprinting before return are the most important prevention steps.

sev.d: Large tear — get a medical assessment first.

INJ.name: Groin (adductor) strain
INJ.what: Strain of the inner thigh muscles, usually from kicking, changing direction or stretching into a split.
signs: Pain in the inner thigh or groin
Pain squeezing the knees together
Pain kicking
flags: Swelling or lump in the groin (possible hernia)
Fever, pain urinating
Deep hip pain with clicking
INJ.note: The Copenhagen plank is one of the most effective groin injury preventers — keep it in your routine for good.

sev.d: Major tear or months of groin pain.

INJ.name: Hip flexor (iliopsoas) strain
INJ.what: Strain of the deep hip flexor at the front of the hip and groin. It hurts to lift the knee, sprint or kick.
signs: Pain at the front of the hip or high groin
Pain lifting the knee against resistance (stairs, sprinting)
Pain when the hip flexor is stretched
flags: Sudden severe pain with a pop and you cannot lift the leg (possible avulsion — common in teenagers)
Fever, or pain that is worse at night
Lump in the groin
INJ.note: Add speed last. Rebuild slow knee-lift strength first, then skips, then sprints and long kicks.

sev.d: Sore at the front of the hip when lifting the knee.
Painful to sprint or kick, weak knee lift.
Big tear or months of front-hip pain.

phases.goal: Walk and climb stairs without pain; gentle activation.
exit: Lifting the knee to hip height 2/10 pain or less

phases.goal: Sprinting, kicking and changes of direction.

INJ.name: Inguinal-related groin pain (sports hernia)
INJ.what: Overload of the lower belly wall just above the groin crease, near the inguinal canal. Common in kicking sports. Usually there is no lump.
signs: Pain in the lower belly or groin crease
Worse with sprinting, kicking or sit-ups
Coughing or sneezing may hurt
flags: A lump in the groin, especially one that gets bigger when you cough (hernia)
Pain in the testicles, or pain passing urine
Fever or feeling unwell
INJ.note: Most athletes recover with exercise in 6–12 weeks. If pain continues after a good programme, ask a sports doctor or surgeon.

sev.d: Pain sprinting, kicking or doing sit-ups.

phases.goal: Calm symptoms; train deep core control.
Hip, groin and trunk strength together.
Back to sprinting, kicking and turning.
exit: Full training and long kicks pain-free

INJ.name: Pubic-related groin pain (osteitis pubis)
INJ.what: Overload of the pubic joint where the two halves of the pelvis meet at the front. Pain is right over the pubic bone and often on both sides.
signs: Pain right over the pubic bone in the middle
Pain on one or both sides of the groin
Worse with kicking, sprinting, sit-ups or getting out of a car
flags: Fever, or feeling unwell (possible bone infection)
Severe pain at night
Pain after childbirth that stops you walking
INJ.note: This settles slowly. Increase load every 1–2 weeks, not every day, and keep pain at 3/10 or less.

sev.d: Sore over the pubic bone after sport.
Walking fast or getting out of a car hurts.

phases.goal: Calm the joint; no long kicks, sprints or sit-ups.

exit: Copenhagen short lever 30 s each side

phases.goal: Running, cutting and kicking step by step.
exit: Full training with no pain the next morning

INJ.name: Hip-related groin pain (impingement / labral tear)
INJ.what: Pain from inside the hip joint, such as hip impingement (FAI) or a tear of the labrum — the cartilage ring around the socket. Felt deep in the groin.
signs: Deep groin pain, sometimes in a 'C' shape around the hip
Clicking, catching or locking in the hip
Pain in deep squats, crossing the legs or long sitting
flags: Hip locks and you cannot move it
Teenager with hip or knee pain and a limp (needs an X-ray)
Fever, or severe night pain
INJ.note: While it is sore, avoid very deep squats and long sitting with knees higher than hips. Use a slightly wider stance with toes turned out.

sev.d: Deep groin ache after sport or long sitting.
Clicking, catching, pain in deep squats.

phases.goal: Pain-free hip control without deep bending.

exit: Single-leg squat to a box with good control
No clicking pain in daily life
Full training without pain the next day

INJ.name: Lower back pain
INJ.what: Most back pain is not from serious damage, even when it hurts a lot. It usually improves within weeks. Staying active is better than bed rest.
signs: Ache or spasm in the lower back
Stiffness in the morning or after sitting
flags: Numbness in the groin or buttocks, or new problems controlling bladder or bowel — go to hospital NOW
Leg weakness getting worse
Fever, unexplained weight loss, history of cancer
Pain after a major fall or accident
INJ.note: Keep moving within comfort. Walking daily helps. Gradually return to lifting — a strong back is a less painful back.

phases.goal: Strength for daily life and sport.

INJ.name: Rotator cuff / shoulder impingement
INJ.what: Pain on the side or front of the shoulder when lifting the arm, from irritation of the rotator cuff tendons. Load management and strengthening work for most people.
signs: Pain lifting the arm overhead
Pain lying on that side
Painful arc between 60° and 120°
flags: Cannot lift the arm at all after a fall (possible tear or dislocation)
Pain with fever or redness
Pain spreading down the arm with numbness
INJ.note: Keep pain during exercise at 3/10 or less. Strength takes 8–12 weeks to change.

sev.d: Pain at night, arm feels weak.

exit: Arm lifts to shoulder height comfortably

phases.goal: Rotator cuff and shoulder blade strength.
Strength overhead and in sport positions.

INJ.name: Tennis elbow
INJ.what: Overload of the forearm tendon on the outer elbow from gripping and wrist extension — common in racket sports and workers.
signs: Pain on the outer elbow when gripping
Pain lifting a cup or kettle
flags: Numbness or tingling in the hand
Swelling or locking of the elbow
Pain after a fall
INJ.note: Change grip size or technique if it comes from sport.

exit: Gripping a cup with little pain
3×15 eccentrics with 2 kg pain 3/10 or less
Full play or work without flare-ups

INJ.name: Knee osteoarthritis (wear & tear)
INJ.what: Gradual changes in the knee cartilage and bone, more common after 40 or after an old injury. It causes pain and stiffness, but the knee responds very well to strength training — exercise is the main treatment.
signs: Stiffness after rest that eases within 30 minutes
Pain on stairs, long walks or getting up from a chair
Grinding or creaking
Swelling after a busy day
flags: Hot, red, swollen knee with fever
Sudden inability to take weight
Knee locking
INJ.note: Mild pain (up to 3–4/10) during exercise is fine if it settles within 24 hours. Losing weight, if overweight, also reduces knee pain.

sev.d: Daily life fine, sport or long walks hurt.
Stairs and standing up are painful.
Daily pain; also discuss options with your doctor.

phases.goal: Reduce pain and stiffness, wake up the thigh muscles.
exit: Walking 20 min with pain 3/10 or less

phases.goal: Stronger quads and hips to take load off the joint.

INJ.name: Osgood-Schlatter (teen knee pain)
INJ.what: Irritation where the kneecap tendon attaches to the growing shin bone. It causes a tender bump just below the kneecap during growth spurts, especially with lots of running and jumping. It is not dangerous and settles when growth finishes.
signs: Tender bony bump below the kneecap
Pain kneeling, jumping or sprinting
Age 10–15 and growing fast
flags: Pain at night or at rest
Fever or a red, hot knee
Whole knee swollen or cannot straighten
INJ.note: Use a pain-guided activity ladder: reduce jumping and sprinting until pain is 2/10 or less, then add back step by step. Total rest is not needed.

phases.goal: Reduce load and pain with holds.

exit: Full training with pain 2/10 or less

INJ.name: Calf strain
INJ.what: A tear in the calf muscles (gastrocnemius or soleus), usually a sudden pull while pushing off or accelerating. Soleus strains can come on more gradually during running.
signs: Sudden sharp pull in the calf
Pain rising onto the toes
Tightness, sometimes bruising
flags: Felt like being kicked in the back of the heel, cannot stand on tiptoe (possible Achilles rupture)
Calf hot, red and swollen, especially after a long journey or surgery (possible blood clot)
INJ.note: Calf strains re-occur often. Before sport you should do 25+ single-leg calf raises and run without pain.

sev.d: Limping, cannot tiptoe on that leg.

INJ.name: Quadriceps (front thigh) strain
INJ.what: A tear in the front thigh muscle, most often from kicking or sprinting. Pain is felt in the front of the thigh.
signs: Sudden pain in the front of the thigh while kicking or sprinting
Pain lifting the knee or straightening against resistance
Pain stretching the front of the thigh
flags: Large, hard, swelling thigh after a hit (do not massage — see a doctor)
Cannot lift the leg at all
INJ.note: Rebuild kicking gradually: short passes first, then long balls and shooting.

INJ.name: Neck pain (desk & phone posture)
INJ.what: Stiff, sore neck muscles, usually not serious. Strengthening the neck and shoulder muscles helps more than stretching alone.
signs: Stiff, sore neck
Worse after long phone or desk time
Headache starting at the base of the skull
flags: Weakness, numbness or tingling spreading down the arm
Dizziness, double vision, trouble speaking or swallowing
Pain after a fall or accident
Fever with a very stiff neck
INJ.note: Move often: every 30–45 minutes of screen time, do a few chin tucks and shoulder rolls. Raise your screen to eye level.

phases.goal: Keep the neck strong for life.

INJ.name: Shoulder dislocation / instability
INJ.what: The shoulder has slipped partly (subluxation) or fully (dislocation) out of its socket. Strong rotator cuff and shoulder-blade muscles are the first-line treatment. Young athletes who dislocate often may need to discuss surgery.
signs: Shoulder 'went out' or felt like it slipped
Fear when the arm goes up and back (throwing position)
Weak or 'dead' arm afterwards
flags: Shoulder still out of place — go to hospital, don't push it back yourself
Numbness in the arm or hand
First dislocation over age 40 (higher chance of rotator cuff tear)
INJ.note: Avoid the arm up-and-back position early. Follow your doctor's advice on sling use.

sev.d: Shoulder slipped but went back by itself.
Fully out, put back in hospital.
Several episodes — also see a specialist.

phases.goal: Settle pain, keep the shoulder blade working.

INJ.name: Sciatica (pain down the leg)
INJ.what: Leg pain that travels from the low back or buttock down the leg, often below the knee, sometimes with tingling. It usually comes from an irritated nerve root, for example from a disc bulge. Most people get better without surgery within weeks to months.
signs: Leg pain, often worse than the back pain
Pain, tingling or numbness below the knee
Worse with sitting, coughing or sneezing
flags: Numbness around the groin or buttocks, or new bladder/bowel problems — go to hospital NOW
Foot or leg getting weaker (foot drop)
Pain in both legs
Fever or unexplained weight loss
INJ.note: Keep moving within comfort and walk daily. If one position (like the prone press-up) makes the leg pain move up towards the back, that's a good sign — do more of it.

sev.d: Can work and walk, some leg pain.
Get a medical review first, then follow this plan.

phases.goal: Reduce leg pain and keep moving.
exit: Leg pain reducing or moving up towards the back

phases.goal: Return to lifting, work and sport.

INJ.name: Stress fracture in the low back (spondylolysis)
INJ.sport: Teen footballers, gymnasts, cricket bowlers, wrestlers
INJ.what: A stress fracture in a small part of a lower vertebra, caused by repeated bending backwards and twisting. It is the most common cause of ongoing back pain in young athletes. It needs a doctor's diagnosis (usually a scan), and most heal with rest from sport and rehab.
signs: Low back pain in an athlete aged 10–20
Worse bending backwards or twisting (kicking, bowling, back walkovers)
Often on one side
flags: Suspected? Stop sport and see a doctor for a scan before starting
Numbness or weakness in the legs
Pain at night or at rest
INJ.note: Avoid backward bending and twisting sport moves until your doctor clears you. Phase 1 is relative rest — everyday activity is fine.

sev.d: Pain for a long time — slower return.

phases.goal: No sport; let the bone heal with gentle core work.

exit: Side plank 45 s each side pain-free

INJ.name: Upper back & posture pain
INJ.what: An ache or stiffness between the shoulder blades, often from long sitting, phone use or heavy training. It is usually muscular and improves with movement and strengthening the upper back.
signs: Ache between the shoulder blades
Stiff after long sitting
Feels better when moving
flags: Chest pain with breathlessness, sweating or pain into the arm or jaw — call an ambulance
Pain after a fall or accident
Fever, night pain or unexplained weight loss
INJ.note: Change position every 30–45 minutes. Strength work for the upper back matters more than 'perfect posture'.

pts: Waiting until at least 9 months after surgery before returning to pivoting sport: each month of delay up to 9 months cut the re-injury rate by about half, and more equal quadriceps strength lowered risk further.
Neuromuscular warm-up programmes (balance, landing and strength drills, like FIFA 11+) roughly halve the risk of ACL injury in athletes.
refs: Grindem et al. 2016, British Journal of Sports Medicine (Delaware-Oslo ACL cohort)
Gagnier et al. 2013, American Journal of Sports Medicine (meta-analysis)
Donnell-Fink et al. 2015, PLoS One (meta-analysis)

pts: An international consensus recommends exercise therapy — especially combined hip and knee strengthening — to reduce pain and improve function in the short, medium and long term.
Foot orthoses can help short-term; massage-type manual therapy and electrotherapy are not recommended.
refs: Crossley et al. 2016, British Journal of Sports Medicine (4th International Patellofemoral Pain consensus)

pts: 12 weeks of heavy slow resistance training gave good short- and long-term results and the highest patient satisfaction; steroid injections helped short-term but results got worse later.
Isometric holds and slow isotonic exercise both reduced in-season tendon pain, with no clear winner — choose what you tolerate.
refs: Kongsgaard et al. 2009, Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports (RCT)
van Ark et al. 2016, Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport (RCT)

pts: For degenerative tears in middle-aged adults, 12 weeks of supervised exercise was as good as keyhole surgery for pain and function at 2 years, and built more thigh strength.
Traumatic tears in young athletes, or a knee that locks, may still need a surgical opinion.
refs: Kise et al. 2016, BMJ (RCT, 140 patients)

pts: Most grade I–II MCL sprains heal without surgery with a period of protection (sometimes a hinged brace) and progressive strengthening.
This is based on clinical practice and cohort studies rather than large randomised trials.
refs: Clinical practice consensus and cohort studies

pts: Few good trials exist. Reducing running load (especially downhill) and strengthening the hip abductors is the usual approach.
Stretching the IT band alone has little support.
refs: Clinical consensus; small trials only

pts: After an ankle sprain, exercise therapy (balance and strength) lowers the odds of spraining again by about 40%.
Wearing a brace or tape during sport lowers the odds of re-injury even more — by about 60%.
The Ottawa ankle rules (bone tenderness or not able to take 4 steps) pick up about 98% of ankle and midfoot fractures, so they tell you when an X-ray is needed.
refs: Doherty et al. 2017, British Journal of Sports Medicine (overview of systematic reviews)
Bachmann et al. 2003, BMJ (systematic review of the Ottawa rules)

pts: Both heavy slow calf training and eccentric heel drops improved Achilles function over 12 weeks, and results lasted to 1 year.
People stuck to the heavy slow programme better (92% vs 78% of sessions).
refs: Beyer et al. 2015, American Journal of Sports Medicine (RCT)

pts: High-load single-leg heel raises with a towel under the toes, done every second day, gave better results than stretching at 3 months.
By 12 months both groups had improved similarly — strength work speeds up recovery.
refs: Rathleff et al. 2015, Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports (RCT)

pts: No treatment has been strongly proven; the available trials are small and have a high risk of bias.
Relative rest from impact, strengthening the lower leg, and a slow graded return to running remain the standard approach.
refs: Winters et al. 2013, Sports Medicine (systematic review)

pts: A rehab programme focused on lengthening exercises got footballers back to play in about 28 days, compared with 51 days for conventional exercises.
Programmes that include the Nordic hamstring exercise cut hamstring injuries by about half.
refs: Askling et al. 2013, British Journal of Sports Medicine (RCT)
van Dyk et al. 2019, British Journal of Sports Medicine (meta-analysis of 8,459 athletes)

pts: A simple Copenhagen adduction programme lowered the risk of groin problems by 41% in football players over a season.
For long-standing adductor-related groin pain, an active strengthening programme beat passive physiotherapy: far more athletes returned to sport.
refs: Harøy et al. 2019, British Journal of Sports Medicine (cluster RCT, 652 players)
Hölmich et al. 1999, The Lancet (RCT)

pts: International guidelines recommend education, staying active and exercise as first-line care.
Bed rest, routine scans, strong painkillers, injections and surgery are overused and should be used carefully.
refs: Foster et al. 2018, The Lancet (Low Back Pain Series)

pts: Keyhole 'decompression' surgery was no better than placebo surgery for this kind of shoulder pain.
Exercise-based rehab is therefore the first-line treatment.
refs: Beard et al. 2018, The Lancet (CSAW placebo-controlled trial)

pts: Physiotherapy (mobilisation plus exercise) beat wait-and-see at 6 weeks.
Steroid injections worked best at 6 weeks, but 72% of patients relapsed and they did worse than physiotherapy at 1 year.
refs: Bisset et al. 2006, BMJ (RCT)

pts: Land-based exercise reduces knee pain and improves function, with effects similar to anti-inflammatory tablets — high-quality evidence.
Exercise, education and weight management are the core recommended treatments.
refs: Fransen et al. 2015, Cochrane review (54 trials)
Bannuru et al. 2019, Osteoarthritis and Cartilage (OARSI guidelines)

pts: A 12-week programme of pain-guided activity changes plus knee and hip strengthening led to 80% of young athletes reporting improvement.
Return to full sport often takes longer, so patience and gradual loading are key.
refs: Rathleff et al. 2020, Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine (cohort study)

pts: Progressive calf loading and criteria-based return (strength and running tests, not just time) are recommended to reduce the high re-injury rate.
Evidence comes mainly from cohort studies and expert consensus in elite sport.
refs: Sports medicine reviews and consensus on calf muscle injuries

pts: Progressive loading, then running and a graded kicking progression, is the recommended approach.
Evidence comes mainly from cohort studies and expert consensus in professional football.
refs: Sports medicine reviews and consensus on muscle injuries

pts: Strengthening the neck, shoulder and upper-back muscles reduces chronic neck pain (moderate-quality evidence).
Stretching alone did not help — combine stretching with strengthening.
refs: Gross et al. 2015, Cochrane review (27 trials)

pts: Rotator cuff and shoulder-blade strengthening is the standard first treatment after a dislocation.
Young athletes have a high chance of it happening again, so repeated dislocations should be discussed with a specialist.
refs: Clinical practice guidelines and cohort studies on shoulder instability

pts: In a large trial, early surgery for sciatica from a disc gave faster leg-pain relief, but after 1 year results were the same as with non-surgical care — about 95% had recovered in both groups.
Staying active and exercise are recommended first; surgery is an option if severe pain persists or weakness develops.
refs: Peul et al. 2007, New England Journal of Medicine (RCT, 283 patients)
Foster et al. 2018, The Lancet (Low Back Pain Series)

pts: About 92% of young athletes with this stress fracture returned to sport with non-surgical treatment (rest from sport plus rehab) — slightly more than after surgery.
Early diagnosis with a scan and rest from backward-bending sport moves are key.
refs: Overley et al. 2017, Global Spine Journal (meta-analysis, 376 patients)

pts: There is little research specifically on upper-back pain. This plan uses the same approach that helps neck pain: mobility plus strengthening of the upper back and shoulder blades.
refs: Gross et al. 2015, Cochrane review (neck exercise) — applied by extension

pts: Iliopsoas-related groin pain is one of the five agreed types of groin pain in athletes; pain lifting the knee against resistance or stretching the hip flexor points to it.
Treatment is based on progressive loading; there are few randomised trials for this specific injury.
refs: Weir et al. 2015, British Journal of Sports Medicine (Doha agreement on groin pain)

pts: In 205 athletes with groin pain, a rehab programme targeting strength and movement control let most return to play after about 10 weeks.
Surgery is considered when a good exercise programme has not worked.
refs: King et al. 2018, British Journal of Sports Medicine (cohort, 205 athletes)
Weir et al. 2015, BJSM (Doha agreement)

pts: Pubic-related groin pain is managed with load reduction and progressive adductor and core strengthening; recovery often takes several months.
Most evidence comes from case series and expert consensus.
refs: Weir et al. 2015, BJSM (Doha agreement)
Expert consensus and case series

pts: In a large trial of hip impingement, both keyhole surgery and a physio-led exercise programme improved pain and function; surgery gave a slightly bigger improvement at 12 months.
Strengthening the hip and core is the first step for most people.
refs: Griffin et al. 2018, The Lancet (UK FASHIoN trial, 348 patients)

PROGS.name: Everyday full-body health
PROGS.sub: For average adults · strength, mobility, heart health
PROGS.why: Adults need muscle-strengthening work at least 2 days a week and 150 minutes of moderate activity. This plan covers both in 15–30 minutes a day.

PROGS.name: Knee & ankle joint care
PROGS.sub: Prevention for footballers, runners and active people
PROGS.why: Strong hips, quads and calves plus good balance and landing technique protect the knees and ankles. Programmes like FIFA 11+ cut lower-limb injuries substantially.

TYPEDESC.Isometric: Holding a contraction without moving — calms pain
TYPEDESC.Strength: Moving against load to rebuild muscle & tendon
TYPEDESC.Plyometric: Hops, jumps and landings for sport

Mobility.speed: Slow and smooth, 2–3 s each way

Stretch.speed: Ease in slowly, then hold still
Stretch.breath: Slow breaths; relax more as you breathe out
Stretch.feel: A gentle stretch that fades a little as you hold

Isometric.breath: Keep breathing; don't hold your breath
Isometric.feel: Muscle working hard, pain should ease

Strength.speed: 2–3 s down, short pause, 1–2 s up
Strength.effort: Hard but controlled — stop with 2 reps left
Strength.breath: Breathe out as you push or lift
Strength.feel: Muscle burn is fine; joint pain should stay 3/10 or less

Core.speed: Slow and controlled; keep the spine still
Core.feel: Tummy and trunk working, not the low back

Balance.speed: Hold steady; small wobbles are normal
Balance.feel: Ankle and hip making small corrections

Plyometric.feel: Springy legs; stop when landings get noisy or knees cave in

Cardio.speed: Steady pace you can keep up
Cardio.effort: Moderate — you can talk but not sing
Cardio.feel: Warm and slightly out of breath

all: Cannot take 4 steps or put any weight on it
Obvious deformity, or the joint looks out of place
Numbness, tingling, or a cold, pale limb
Fever, or the joint is hot, red and very swollen
Severe pain at night or at rest that never eases
back: Numbness around the groin or buttocks, or new problems controlling bladder or bowel
Weakness in the legs that is getting worse
Chest pain with breathlessness or sweating
neck: Dizziness, double vision, or trouble speaking or swallowing
Weakness or numbness spreading down an arm
knee: Knee locked — cannot straighten it fully
ankle: Felt like being kicked in the back of the heel and cannot stand on tiptoe
shin: One small spot on the bone is very painful to touch
Calf is hot, red and swollen (especially after travel or surgery)
thigh: Thigh is large, hard and swelling after a hit
hip: A lump in the groin that gets bigger when you cough
Teenager with a limp and hip or knee pain

meniscus.part: The meniscus is a C-shaped cushion of cartilage between the thigh bone and the shin bone. Each knee has two — inner (medial) and outer (lateral). They absorb shock and help keep the knee steady.
meniscus.how: Usually a twist on a bent knee with the foot planted — turning to pass, or rotating while squatting. After about 35, tears can also appear slowly with everyday wear.
grades: A small split near the edge. The knee still bends and straightens fully. Most settle with exercise in 4–8 weeks.
Swelling after activity, catching or clicking, deep squats hurt. Exercise is still usually the first treatment; some people need a scan.
A torn flap blocks the knee so it can't straighten. See a doctor soon — this often needs keyhole surgery.
meniscus.heal: The outer third of the meniscus has a blood supply and can heal. The inner part heals poorly, but the knee copes very well when the muscles around it are strong. For wear-type tears, 12 weeks of exercise worked as well as surgery.
muscles: Your main shock absorber — strong quads take load off the meniscus.
Control the hip so the knee doesn't twist or cave inward.
Keeps the knee in line when you land or squat on one leg.
Protect the back of the knee and control rotation.
Absorb force when you run and land.
stronger: Increase squat depth slowly — pain should stay at 3/10 or less and settle by the next day.
Practise soft landings with the knee over the middle toes.
Keep 2 leg-strength sessions a week even after you're back to sport.

acl.part: The ACL (anterior cruciate ligament) is a strong band in the centre of the knee. It stops the shin bone sliding forward and twisting under the thigh bone.
acl.how: Most ACL tears happen without contact: landing from a jump, stopping suddenly or cutting with the knee caving inward. Many people feel or hear a 'pop' and the knee swells within a few hours.
grades: Fibres stretched but the knee is stable.
Some fibres torn; the knee may feel unsteady.
The most common type. The ligament is torn through and the knee can give way when turning.
acl.heal: A completely torn ACL does not grow back together by itself. Some people return to sport with rehab alone; many athletes choose reconstruction surgery. Either way, rehab takes 9 months or more — returning to cutting sports earlier greatly raises the risk of another tear.
muscles: Act like a 'second ACL' — they pull the shin bone back and stop it sliding forward.
Need to be rebuilt to equal the other leg; weak quads are the biggest re-injury risk.
Stop the knee from caving inward when landing and cutting.
Side-hip strength keeps the knee lined up over the foot.
Help absorb landings and protect the knee.
Keeps your body balanced over the knee when you change direction.
stronger: Test before you return: both legs should hop and lift almost equally (90%+).
Train landing and cutting technique — knees over toes, soft bend.
Keep a warm-up like FIFA 11+ forever; it roughly halves ACL injuries.

mcl.part: The MCL (medial collateral ligament) is a strap on the inner side of the knee. It stops the knee bending inward.
mcl.how: A hit to the outside of the knee (a tackle) or the knee collapsing inward when landing or skiing.
grades: Stretched — tender on the inner knee but stable. Usually 1–3 weeks.
Partly torn — some looseness and pain bending. Usually 3–6 weeks, sometimes with a brace.
Fully torn — the knee opens on the inner side. Often happens with an ACL tear; see a doctor.
mcl.heal: The MCL has a good blood supply, so it usually heals without surgery. Gentle movement and progressive strength help the new fibres line up strongly.
muscles: Support the knee and restore full straightening.
The inner-thigh muscles sit right next to the MCL and help protect the inner knee.
Stops the knee collapsing inward — the movement that injures the MCL.
Add stability on the inner and back of the knee.
stronger: Return to side-to-side movement gradually: walk, jog, then cut.
Strengthen the inner thigh (adductors) and side hip twice a week.
Use a hinged brace for contact sport only if your doctor or physio advises it.

groin.part: The adductors are the inner-thigh muscles that pull your legs together. The adductor longus is the one most often strained, usually close to where it attaches to the pubic bone.
groin.how: Kicking hard, changing direction quickly, or slipping into a split. Also builds up slowly when training load jumps.
grades: A few fibres strained — tight and sore when kicking. 1–3 weeks.
Partial tear — pain walking fast, weak squeeze. 3–8 weeks.
Big tear, or groin pain for months. Needs a structured programme; see a sports doctor if not improving.
groin.heal: Muscle tissue heals in a few weeks, but the tendon near the bone is slower. Strengthening (not just rest and stretching) is what works — active training beat passive treatment for long-standing groin pain.
muscles: The injured muscles — make them strong with squeezes and the Copenhagen plank.
Abs and obliques share the load across the pelvis with the adductors.
Balance the hip so the inner thigh isn't overworked.
Often tight and weak together with the adductors in kicking sports.
stronger: Keep the Copenhagen plank in your weekly routine — it cut groin problems by 41% in footballers.
Build kicking and sprint volume gradually after time off.
Test your squeeze: both sides should feel equally strong.

hipflexor.part: The iliopsoas is the deep hip flexor. It runs from the lower spine and inside of the pelvis, over the front of the hip, to the top of the thigh bone. It lifts your knee.
hipflexor.how: Sprinting, kicking, or suddenly lifting the knee against resistance — common in football, running and martial arts.
grades: Sore at the front of the hip when lifting the knee. 1–3 weeks.
Painful to sprint or kick, weak knee lift. 3–6 weeks.
Big tear or months of pain. See a sports doctor.
hipflexor.heal: The muscle heals in a few weeks when loaded gradually. Pain stretching the hip flexor or lifting the knee against your hand points to this type of groin pain.
muscles: Rebuild knee-lift strength slowly, then speed.
Stabilises the lower spine where the iliopsoas attaches.
Strong glutes balance the front of the hip.
Work closely with the hip flexors in kicking.
stronger: Add speed last: slow strength first, then skips, then sprints.
Warm up the hip flexors before kicking or sprinting.
Avoid long sitting without breaks; move every 45 minutes.

inguinal.part: The inguinal canal is a natural passage through the lower belly wall, just above the crease of the groin. In 'inguinal-related groin pain' (sometimes called a sports hernia) the muscles and tissues around it are overloaded — usually there is no lump.
inguinal.how: Repeated kicking, sprinting and twisting, often with a weak or tired core. Pain often comes on slowly.
grades: Pain during sprinting, kicking or sit-ups; coughing or sneezing may hurt.
Pain for months. Most improve with 6–12 weeks of exercise; a few need a surgeon's opinion.
inguinal.heal: Most athletes recover with a programme that strengthens the core and hips and improves movement control — in one large study players returned to sport after about 10 weeks of rehab.
muscles: The key area — deep abs and obliques protect the lower belly wall.
Often weak at the same time; balance them with the core.
Control the pelvis when you kick and change direction.
Train them without overloading the groin.
stronger: A visible or hard lump in the groin is a hernia — see a doctor.
Train the core with control exercises (dead bug, Pallof press) before crunches.
Increase kicking distance and sprint speed step by step.

pubic.part: The pubic joint (pubic symphysis) is where the two halves of the pelvis meet at the front. In pubic-related groin pain the bone and joint are overloaded and irritated (sometimes called osteitis pubis).
pubic.how: Too much kicking, sprinting and change of direction without enough recovery, often when the adductors and core are weak.
grades: Tender over the pubic bone after training.
Pain on both sides of the groin, walking fast or getting out of a car hurts.
Pain for months; can take 3–6 months to settle with careful loading.
pubic.heal: Bone and joint stress settles slowly. Reduce the movements that hurt (long kicks, sprints, sit-ups), keep training what you can, and rebuild adductor and core strength step by step.
muscles: Pull on the pubic bone from below — strong adductors spread the load.
Pull from above — balance between abs and adductors protects the joint.
Stabilise the pelvis when you run.
stronger: Patience: progress loading every 1–2 weeks, not every day.
Keep pain during training at 3/10 or less and settled by the next morning.
See a doctor if pain is severe at night or you have fever.

hiprelated.part: The hip is a ball-and-socket joint. The labrum is a ring of cartilage around the socket. Hip impingement (FAI) is when the ball and socket pinch at the end of movement, which can irritate or tear the labrum.
hiprelated.how: Deep squatting, twisting and kicking, often in people whose hip shape is naturally a bit different. Pain is deep in the groin and may click or catch.
grades: Deep groin ache after sport or long sitting.
Clicking, catching, pain in deep squats or crossing the legs.
Follow your surgeon's limits — a slower plan.
hiprelated.heal: A 3-month physio-led programme improves pain and function for many people; some need keyhole surgery. Strength and control around the hip reduce pinching.
muscles: Controls the hip so the ball doesn't drift into the pinching position.
Strong glutes take load away from the front of the hip.
Pelvic control changes the hip angle in sport.
Balance the inner thigh with the side hip.
stronger: Avoid very deep squats and long sitting with knees above hips while it is sore.
Choose a slightly wider stance and turned-out toes for squats.
A specialist should check hips that keep locking or catching.

pfps.part: The kneecap glides in a groove at the front of the thigh bone. Smooth cartilage lines the back of the kneecap. In runner's knee the joint behind the kneecap is overloaded and irritated — nothing is torn.
pfps.how: Load rising faster than the knee can handle: more running or jumping, hills, stairs, or deep squats. Weak hips and thigh muscles let the knee drift inward, adding stress behind the kneecap.
grades: Ache only after running or jumping; daily life normal.
Stairs, squatting and long sitting hurt.
Pain for over 3 months. Still very treatable with exercise; it just takes longer.
pfps.heal: Because nothing is damaged, the pain settles when load and strength are balanced again. Combined hip and knee strengthening is the best-proven treatment, with results in 6–12 weeks.
muscles: Hold the kneecap in its groove and absorb force.
Stops the knee drifting inward — a key cause of kneecap pain.
Take load away from the knee on stairs and landings.
Absorb impact when running so the knee doesn't have to.
stronger: Cut back (don't stop) running while you strengthen — about 50–70% of normal.
Shorten your stride slightly or increase cadence by 5–10%.
Keep hip exercises twice a week to stop it returning.

patellar.part: The patellar tendon joins the kneecap to the shin bone. Every jump and landing pulls on it. In jumper's knee the tendon fibres just below the kneecap are overloaded and become thicker and sore.
patellar.how: Lots of jumping, landing and sprinting, especially after a sudden increase in training or a new hard surface.
grades: Pain on stairs and in daily life; can take 3–6 months.
patellar.heal: Tendons get stronger with heavy, slow loading — not rest. Total rest makes them weaker and the pain returns when you jump again. Expect 12 weeks of steady progress.
muscles: The muscle that pulls on the tendon — slow heavy squats rebuild the whole unit.
Share landing forces so the tendon takes less.
Balance the knee and help control landings.
stronger: Pain up to 3/10 during loading is OK if it settles by the next morning.
Add jumping back in steps: 2–3 days a week, not daily.
Keep one heavy leg session a week in the season.

itbs.part: The IT band is a thick strip of tissue running down the outside of the thigh from the hip to just below the knee. In IT band syndrome the tissue where it crosses the outer knee becomes irritated.
itbs.how: Repeated knee bending in running or cycling — usually after a jump in distance, lots of downhill running, or weak hip muscles letting the knee drop inward.
grades: Pain within the first 1–2 km or on stairs.
Pain stops running completely. Seek a physio assessment.
itbs.heal: It settles when running load is reduced and the hips get stronger. Foam rolling and stretching may feel good but do not fix it on their own.
muscles: Keeps the pelvis level and the knee from dropping inward when you run.
Control hip rotation and share the load.
Support the knee on downhill running.
Keeps your pelvis stable on every stride.
stronger: Reduce distance and avoid downhill running until pain-free.
Run on alternating sides of a sloped road, or on flat ground.
Increase weekly distance by about 10% at a time.

knee-oa.part: In knee osteoarthritis the smooth cartilage that covers the ends of the bones slowly thins, the joint space narrows and small bone spurs can form at the edges. The knee keeps adapting and repairing — it is not simply 'worn out'.
knee-oa.how: Age, an old knee injury (for example ACL or meniscus), extra body weight and genetics all play a part. It develops over years.
grades: Daily life is fine; long walks or sport hurt.
Pain most days on stairs or standing up.
Pain at rest or at night. Still keep exercising; also talk to your doctor about other options.
knee-oa.heal: Exercise is the main, most-recommended treatment: strength and activity reduce pain about as much as common painkillers. Cartilage loves movement — joints are nourished when they are loaded.
muscles: The most important — stronger quads mean less knee pain and better walking.
Make standing up and stairs easier.
Reduces the inward knee load that hurts the inner joint.
stronger: Mild pain (3–4/10) during exercise is fine if it settles within 24 hours.
Walk most days; use a cycle or pool on flare-up days.
If overweight, losing 5–10% of body weight clearly reduces knee pain.

osgood.part: In growing children, the patellar tendon attaches to a growth area at the top of the shin bone (the tibial tuberosity). In Osgood-Schlatter this growth area is pulled and irritated, making a tender bump below the kneecap.
osgood.how: Growth spurts plus lots of running, jumping and kicking. The bones grow fast and the muscles become tight and pull harder on the growth area.
grades: Stairs and kneeling hurt in daily life.
osgood.heal: It is not dangerous and settles when growth finishes (usually by 14–16). The bump may stay but stops hurting. Managing load — not total rest — keeps young players active.
muscles: Gentle strength (and later stretching) reduces the pull on the growth area.
Help with landing so the knee takes less.
Balance the front and back of the thigh.
stronger: Use the pain ladder: keep sport pain at 2/10 or less.
Use knee pads for kneeling and goalkeeping.
Talk to the coach about fewer jumping and sprint drills during growth spurts.

ankle-sprain.part: The outer ankle has three small ligaments that hold the ankle bones together. The one at the front (ATFL) is injured in almost every sprain; bad sprains also tear the one below (CFL).
ankle-sprain.how: The foot rolls inward — landing on someone's foot, stepping on uneven ground or turning quickly. Swelling and bruising appear on the outer ankle.
grades: Little swelling; you can walk with mild pain. 1–3 weeks.
Clear swelling and bruising, limping. 3–6 weeks.
Large swelling, the ankle feels unstable and walking is very hard. 6–12 weeks; get it checked.
ankle-sprain.heal: Ligaments heal by laying down new fibres over 6–12 weeks. Early movement, walking as able and balance training make them stronger. Without proper rehab, up to 1 in 3 people sprain the same ankle again.
muscles: Strong calves control the ankle when you land and push off.
Shin muscles pull the foot up and steady it on landing.
Small foot muscles improve balance on uneven ground.
Hip control reduces how hard you land on the ankle.
stronger: Balance on one leg every day — eyes closed when it gets easy.
Keep balance and hop drills for 3 months after you are back.
Consider a brace or tape for sport in the first year after a bad sprain.

achilles.part: The Achilles tendon joins the calf muscles to the heel bone. It is the strongest tendon in the body. In tendinopathy the tendon is overloaded and thickens — most often 2–6 cm above the heel.
achilles.how: A rise in running, jumping or hill training, new shoes, or a hard surface — often in people over 30 when the tendon recovers more slowly.
grades: Stiff in the morning, fine once warm.
Pain walking, thickened tendon. Can take 3–6 months.
achilles.heal: Tendons rebuild with steady, heavy calf loading over about 12 weeks. Rest alone makes them weaker. Pain up to 3–4/10 during loading is acceptable if it settles by the next morning.
muscles: The core treatment — heavy calf raises with straight and bent knees.
Help push off so the calf and tendon aren't overloaded.
Power for running that spares the lower leg.
Stable feet reduce twisting load on the tendon.
stronger: Keep 2 calf-strength sessions a week forever.
Increase running by about 10% a week; add hills last.
Morning stiffness is your guide: if it is worse the next day, ease off.

plantar.part: The plantar fascia is a thick band under the foot. It runs from the heel bone to the base of the toes and supports the arch. In plantar fasciitis (heel pain) the band is overloaded where it attaches to the heel.
plantar.how: Long standing or walking, a jump in running, weight gain, tight calves or worn-out shoes.
grades: Long-standing heel pain — still improves with loading.
plantar.heal: Most people get better within 6–12 months, faster with the right exercise. High-load heel raises with the toes lifted strengthen the band itself; a supportive shoe and calf stretches also help.
muscles: Tight, weak calves pull on the heel and fascia.
Small foot muscles support the arch with the fascia.
Shin muscles help hold the arch.
Better leg control spreads the load when you walk and run.
stronger: Do the high-load heel raise (towel under toes) every other day.
Wear supportive shoes; avoid long barefoot walking on hard floors while sore.
Stretch the calf and arch before the first steps in the morning.

shin.part: Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) is overload of the inner edge of the shin bone and the muscles attached to it, usually along the lower half.
shin.how: A sudden jump in running, new hard surfaces, or worn shoes — common in new runners, football pre-season and military training.
grades: Pain after running; eases during the run.
Pain walking or at rest — rule out a stress fracture first.
shin.heal: Bone adapts to load over weeks. Reduce running enough to keep pain low, then build up slowly. One small, very painful spot on the bone can be a stress fracture — see a doctor.
muscles: Soleus and calf strength absorb running shock before the bone.
Shin muscles control the foot landing.
Arch strength reduces strain on the inner shin.
Help with running form and load.
stronger: Increase running by no more than 10% a week.
Mix running surfaces and replace worn shoes.
Run with slightly shorter, quicker steps.

calf.part: The calf has two main muscles: the gastrocnemius (the bulky upper calf) and the soleus (deeper and lower). A calf strain is a tear in one of them — most often the inner gastrocnemius.
calf.how: A sudden push-off or acceleration ('like being hit in the calf'), often in tennis and football, and more common over 35. Soleus strains can come on gradually while running.
grades: Tight; you can walk normally. 1–3 weeks.
Limping; can't rise onto tiptoe on that leg. 3–6 weeks.
Large tear — get checked by a doctor first.
calf.heal: Muscle heals in weeks. Gentle early walking and calf raises help the new fibres line up strongly. Rushing back to sprinting is the main cause of re-tears.
muscles: Rebuild both the bent-knee (soleus) and straight-knee (gastrocnemius) parts.
Power for running so the calf takes less.
Better foot control reduces strain on the calf.
stronger: Warm up with skips and calf raises before sprinting.
Return to sprinting step by step: 60%, 80%, then 100%.
Keep 2 calf sessions a week, especially if you are over 35.

hamstring.part: The hamstrings are three muscles at the back of the thigh. The outer one (biceps femoris) is torn most often, usually in its upper part where muscle joins tendon.
hamstring.how: Sprinting at top speed — the muscle is stretched and working hard at the same moment as the leg swings forward. Also from high kicks or slipping into a split. Fatigue and a previous tear raise the risk.
grades: Tight, can walk and jog. 1–3 weeks.
Clear pain, limping, maybe bruising. 3–8 weeks.
Large tear or tendon pulled off the bone (often with a pop near the buttock) — see a doctor first.
hamstring.heal: Muscle repairs in weeks, but strength and sprint speed take longer to return. Most re-injuries happen when players go back before full strength. The Nordic hamstring curl halves hamstring injuries.
muscles: Rebuild strength at long muscle length — Nordics and single-leg deadlifts.
Strong glutes do more of the sprint work, sparing the hamstrings.
Pelvic control stops the hamstrings being over-stretched.
stronger: Return to sprinting step by step: 60%, 80%, 90%, then full speed.
Keep Nordic curls once or twice a week all season.
Don't sprint at full speed when very tired at first.

quad.part: The quadriceps are four muscles at the front of the thigh. The rectus femoris — the long one down the middle — is the one usually torn, because it crosses both the hip and the knee.
quad.how: Kicking hard (especially long balls) or sprinting, often in a cold or tired muscle.
grades: Painful walking fast, weak kick. 3–6 weeks.
Large tear or dent in the muscle — medical assessment first.
quad.heal: The muscle heals in weeks when loaded gradually. Kicking returns last: short passes first, then long kicks.
muscles: Rebuild strength through knee extension and lunges, then speed.
Train the hip-flexing part of rectus femoris for kicking.
Balance the front of the hip.
stronger: Warm up with gradual kicking before shooting or long passes.
Rebuild kicking: 10 m, 20 m, 30 m, then shooting.
Don't stretch hard into pain in the first week.

lbp.part: The lower back has five vertebrae, discs between them, small joints at the back, and layers of muscle. With most back pain no serious damage is found — muscles and joints are sensitive and protective, and the back is still strong.
lbp.how: Lifting, bending, a long day sitting, poor sleep or stress can all trigger it. Often there is no single cause.
grades: A recent flare-up — usually improves within weeks.
Not settling on its own; active treatment helps.
Long-term pain. Exercise, activity and good sleep are the best tools.
lbp.heal: Most episodes improve within 2–6 weeks. Staying active beats bed rest; scans rarely change what helps. Exercise of almost any type you enjoy reduces pain and stops it coming back.
muscles: Deep trunk muscles support the spine in everyday movements.
Strong hips mean the back does less of the lifting.
Back muscles need strength, not just rest.
Better hip bending takes strain off the back.
stronger: Keep moving: short walks every day during a flare-up.
Lift with your hips and legs, close to the body — but bending your back is normal and safe.
Get help urgently for numbness around the groin or bladder/bowel changes.

sciatica.part: Sciatica is pain from an irritated nerve root as it leaves the lower spine. Usually a bulging disc presses on or inflames the nerve, and pain travels down the buttock and leg along the nerve.
sciatica.how: Often after lifting or bending, sometimes for no clear reason. Leg pain is usually worse than back pain, and may come with tingling or numbness.
grades: Leg pain comes and goes; you can work and walk.
Constant leg pain; sitting and sleeping are hard.
Numbness or weakness — get a medical review first.
sciatica.heal: Most people improve within 6–12 weeks; the disc bulge often shrinks by itself. Gentle movement and nerve-glide exercises help. Surgery is only for severe weakness or pain that does not improve.
muscles: Supports the spine so the nerve is less irritated.
Reduce strain on the back during walking and lifting.
Gentle back extension often eases disc-type leg pain.
Gentle mobility helps the nerve glide.
stronger: Find positions that ease leg pain and use them often.
Walk regularly — short and frequent beats long and rare.
Go to hospital now for numbness around the groin or new bladder/bowel problems.

spondy.part: A stress fracture in a small bridge of bone at the back of a lower vertebra (the pars), most often L5. It is the most common cause of ongoing back pain in young athletes.
spondy.how: Repeated bending backwards and twisting — fast bowling, gymnastics, football kicking, wrestling — during growth.
grades: Caught early, before a full crack.
Crack seen on a scan — typical 3–4 month programme.
Pain for over 6 months — slower return.
spondy.heal: With a break from bending backwards and twisting, most heal or settle within 3–6 months. A gradual, supervised return keeps it from coming back.
muscles: Holds the spine steady so the pars is protected.
Power for kicking and bowling without arching the back.
Tight hamstrings increase strain on the low back.
Tight hip flexors tilt the pelvis and arch the back.
stronger: Avoid back-arching moves until your doctor clears you.
Build core endurance (planks, dead bugs) before sport.
Limit bowling or high-load repetitions during growth spurts.

shoulder.part: The rotator cuff is four small muscles whose tendons wrap around the ball of the shoulder and keep it centred in the socket. The top tendon (supraspinatus) runs under the bony roof of the shoulder (acromion) and is the one usually irritated.
shoulder.how: Repeated lifting, throwing or overhead work, or a sudden rise in gym training. Weak shoulder-blade muscles and stiff upper back let the tendon get squeezed and overloaded.
grades: Pain only when throwing or working overhead.
Dressing and reaching up hurt; painful arc lifting the arm sideways.
Pain at night and a weak arm. A sudden loss of strength after a fall needs a doctor (possible tear).
shoulder.heal: Tendon pain improves with progressive strengthening over 6–12 weeks. Exercise gives results similar to surgery for most people with impingement-type pain.
muscles: The rotator cuff itself — band external and internal rotation.
Shoulder-blade muscles give the cuff a stable base.
Strong shoulders share the lifting load.
A stable trunk improves throwing and lifting technique.
stronger: Work in a pain-free range first, then raise the arm higher week by week.
Balance pushing exercises with pulling (rows, Y-raises).
Warm up the cuff with a band before throwing or overhead lifting.

instab.part: The shoulder is a shallow ball-and-socket joint. A ring of cartilage (the labrum) deepens the socket. In a dislocation the ball comes out of the socket — usually forwards — and can tear the labrum and stretch the capsule.
instab.how: A fall on an outstretched arm, or the arm forced up and back (tackling, blocking a shot, wrestling). Young athletes have the highest chance of it happening again.
grades: Slipped and went back by itself.
Fully out and put back by a doctor.
Several episodes — also see a shoulder specialist.
instab.heal: The torn labrum and stretched capsule need muscle control to protect them. Many people regain a stable shoulder with rehab; young contact athletes with repeated dislocations are often offered surgery.
muscles: Keeps the ball centred in the socket — the key protector.
Positions the socket under the ball.
Controls the arm in front of the body (push-ups, tackling).
stronger: Avoid the arm up-and-back position until strength returns.
Build strength in the at-risk position slowly before contact sport.
Any new dislocation means a medical check.

tennis-elbow.part: Tennis elbow is overload of the tendon where the wrist-extensor muscles attach to the bony bump on the outer elbow (lateral epicondyle). These muscles lift the wrist and help you grip.
tennis-elbow.how: Repeated gripping and wrist work — racket sports, tools, carrying bags, typing or a mouse. Only a few cases come from tennis.
grades: Lifting a cup or kettle hurts.
Pain for over 3 months — still improves with loading.
tennis-elbow.heal: Most cases settle within a year, faster with tendon loading exercises. Steroid injections help short-term but results are worse later — exercise is the better long-term choice.
muscles: Slow, heavy wrist-extension loading is the main treatment.
A strong shoulder takes strain off the forearm.
Better arm position for gripping and lifting.
stronger: Lift and carry with the palm facing up when you can.
Use a thicker grip on tools and rackets.
Keep wrist exercises 2–3 times a week after it settles.

neck.part: The neck has seven small vertebrae with discs between them, joints at the back, and layers of muscles that hold up the head. With most neck pain no damage is found — the muscles and joints are sensitive and stiff.
neck.how: Long phone or desk time with the head forward, poor sleep, stress, or a sudden awkward movement.
grades: A recent stiff neck — usually improves within weeks.
Long-term pain — strength, movement and breaks are key.
neck.heal: Most neck pain improves within weeks. Gentle movement and strengthening the deep neck and upper-back muscles help more than rest or a collar.
muscles: Deep neck muscles hold the head without strain.
Shoulder-blade muscles support the neck from below.
Arm strength reduces load on the neck when lifting.
stronger: Hold the phone at eye level; screen at eye height.
Move your neck gently every 30–45 minutes.
See a doctor for dizziness, arm weakness or numbness.

upperback.part: Between the shoulder blades sit the rhomboids and the middle and lower trapezius. With long sitting they become tired and sore, and the upper back stiffens. Nothing is damaged.
upperback.how: Hours of sitting, phone use or driving with rounded shoulders, plus little upper-body strength training.
grades: Months of ache — strength and movement breaks help most.
upperback.heal: Moving the stiff upper back and strengthening the muscles between the shoulder blades usually helps within weeks.
muscles: Rhomboids and trapezius — rows and Y-raises.
Shoulder control for good arm position.
Supports an upright posture without effort.
Stretch and balance tight chest muscles.
stronger: Change position every 30–45 minutes; no single posture is perfect.
Do rows or band pull-aparts 3 times a week.
Set your screen at eye height.
